ACKY: About twenty US stocks copied from the publicly disclosed holdings of a prominent activist investor, plus an options program targeting a 15 percent yearly distribution rate. It lets anyone shadow a famous activist portfolio, with the options adding income and some drag on gains.
ACVT: Convertible securities, the hybrid bonds that pay interest but can turn into stock when the issuer's shares rise, mostly from US companies. They offer a middle path: bond like income with a built in share of stock upside, and less downside cushion than their fans sometimes expect.
AIYY: An options income strategy tied to a small artificial intelligence software company, using contracts that give indirect exposure to its share price while collecting premiums for payouts. It is an income play on one speculative, fast moving stock, with gains capped and losses largely open.
ALTY: Five flavors of alternative income in one fund: real estate trusts, energy partnerships, preferred shares, option strategies and other high payout assets from around the world. It collects income from corners a normal stock and bond mix misses, though its holdings can be volatile and complex.
AOCT: Options on the S&P 500 set for a two year outcome period ending in October 2028, designed to protect against losses on large US stocks over that whole stretch in exchange for capped gains. The longer term suits investors who want protection planned years ahead, not reset annually.
APRT: Options on the S&P 500 set each April for a one year outcome period, absorbing the first 10 percent of losses while capping gains. Like other buffer funds it trades strong rally potential for a known cushion, and the terms reset every April.
BAMA: A fund of funds holding other ETFs across US and foreign stocks, bonds and cash, shifted actively to wherever the manager sees opportunity. It works as a moderate, one stop allocation, and its results ride on the manager's asset picking rather than any fixed recipe.
BAMO: A fund of funds holding other ETFs across stocks, bonds and cash worldwide, with the freedom to use leverage when the manager sees opportunity. It aims higher than a cautious balanced fund, and the borrowed exposure can magnify both gains and losses.
BCFN: Financial companies built on new technology: banking, lending, payments, insurance, market data and wealth platforms that develop or heavily use innovative tech. It skips the stodgiest corners of finance for its disruptors, making it a growth leaning take on the money business.
CPNJ: Options on the Nasdaq-100 set up each June for a one year outcome period, designed to guard against losses on the tech heavy growth basket while keeping a capped share of gains. It suits investors who want Nasdaq exposure with the downside planned in advance, accepting smaller rallies.
CPSD: Options on the S&P 500 set up each December for a one year outcome period, designed to guard against losses on large US stocks while keeping a capped share of any gains. It suits investors who want stock exposure with the downside planned in advance, accepting that strong rallies will pass it by.
DARP: A concentrated portfolio of thirty to sixty growth companies chosen for innovation and disruption, across technology, media, industry and energy, at home and abroad. It is a conviction driven growth bet, so it swings harder than diversified growth funds when its themes fall in or out of favor.
DCMT: Broad commodity exposure managed actively: energy, industrial and precious metals and farm goods, held through futures and related investments with a view across a full market cycle. It aims to profit from commodity trends over time, offering diversification that moves differently from stocks and bonds.
DDFM: Options on the S&P 500 built to gain from moves in either direction over a one year period starting each March, up to a limit on down moves, while absorbing the first 15 percent of losses. It is a defined outcome holding for investors who want some return even if stocks drift down.
DIVE: A concentrated list of about twenty five to thirty five dividend paying US stocks across most industries, picked for income plus long term growth. Holding few names makes each pick matter, and the dividend focus tilts it toward proven, cash generating companies.
DVLU: About fifty US stocks chosen by blending two signals: strong price momentum and low prices relative to value measures, drawn from large and mid sized companies. The mix tries to buy cheap stocks that are already rising, and it reshuffles as the signals change.
EMSF: Emerging market companies that pass sustainability tests, chosen actively across Asian technology, banks, industry and consumer names in the developing world. It pairs growth in emerging economies with environmental and social screens, so some big state linked and heavy industry names are left out.
FEBM: Options on the S&P 500 set each February for a one year outcome period, designed to provide the maximum loss buffer the options market allows at the time in exchange for capped gains. It prioritizes protection above all, so it will lag badly in strong bull markets.
FFLS: US stocks held both long and short at once, buying companies the managers expect to rise and betting against those they expect to fall, across all sizes. The short book hedges part of the market risk, aiming for returns driven by stock picking rather than the market's direction.
FGSM: Small companies from around the world, with at least 40 percent of its money outside the US across three or more countries, spanning industry, finance, consumer and technology names. It hunts overlooked little firms globally, carrying the extra swings and currency moves that come with small foreign stocks.
FLN: Latin American companies screened for growth and value traits, led by banks with utilities, industrials and materials behind, across Brazil, Mexico and their neighbors. It is a focused bet on the region's economies, carrying extra political and currency swings on top of stock risk.
GGME: Companies shaping next generation media and gaming: video game makers, streaming and social platforms, and the technology behind interactive entertainment, split between tech and communication names. It is a focused growth bet on how people play and watch, swinging with hit titles and user trends.
GSUI: A trust holding Sui, the token of a newer blockchain network built for fast, cheap transactions, that also stakes its holdings to earn extra tokens. It offers stock market access to a young cryptocurrency whose price is highly speculative and swings sharply.
HYUP: The higher beta slice of the high yield bond market: junk bonds that historically swing more than the junk market itself when credit conditions change. It pays junk level income with extra drama, amplifying both the good stretches and the sell-offs of ordinary high yield funds.
IBGC: US Treasury bonds that all mature around December 2046, packaged like a single very long government bond with a known end date. Its long horizon makes its price swing hard when interest rates move, suiting investors matching money to a far future goal.
ITDH: A target date fund for retirement around 2060, holding other funds that mix global stocks and bonds, starting growth heavy and gliding toward safety as the date nears. It is a whole retirement plan in one ticker for young savers, with the mix adjusting itself over decades.
KGRN: Chinese clean technology companies: solar panel makers, electric vehicle and battery firms, wind and clean power generators, with utilities the biggest slice. It is a focused bet on China's green buildout, swinging with energy policy and fierce price competition in that industry.
KTEC: The thirty largest technology companies listed in Hong Kong: internet platforms, e-commerce, phone and chip makers and other Chinese tech leaders. Consumer and media names bulk large alongside pure tech, making it a concentrated bet on China's internet economy and its regulators.
LOHA: Companies built on heavy assets that are hard to replace: pipelines, factories, stores, ships and other long lived physical plant, across industry, retail, energy and food. The idea favors businesses protected by the sheer cost of copying them, a sturdier corner of the stock market.
LOTI: A balanced tactical mix: dividend leaning stocks, with health care and utilities among them, plus bond funds, shifting the split as the manager reads markets. It aims for income with moderate growth, and the tactical freedom means its risk level can drift up or down over time.
MARS: Space industry companies: rocket launchers, satellite makers and operators, space infrastructure and the technology suppliers behind them, mostly industrial firms. It is a focused bet on the commercial space race, a young industry where a few contract wins or launch failures move prices sharply.
MYCG: Corporate bonds that all come due in 2027, packaged like a single company bond with a known end date, paying interest until the bonds mature and return principal. It suits savers matching money to a goal around 2027, and its swings shrink as the date nears.
NMB: Investment grade municipal bonds from across the US, picked actively for the best balance of income, quality and value, with interest generally free from federal income tax. As an actively managed national muni fund it can roam maturities and issuers that index funds cannot.
NYSX: The one hundred largest companies listed on the New York Stock Exchange, led heavily by technology with media and consumer growth names behind. Despite the old exchange's blue chip image, the list is growth tilted today, so it behaves much like a big tech heavy growth fund.
OCTB: Options on a large US stock fund in a structured outcome design that starts each October, absorbing a slice of losses over its outcome period in exchange for capped gains. It offers stock exposure with a planned cushion, suiting investors who prefer knowing the trade off in advance.
OVB: Investment grade US bonds held through other funds, with an options overlay sold on top to add extra income beyond the bonds' own interest. The overlay is the twist on a core bond holding: more payout potential, paid for with added complexity and some upside given away.
PSCX: Options on the S&P 500 in a conservative structured outcome design starting each January, cushioning losses while keeping only part of any gains. The conservative tilt favors protection over participation, suiting investors who want stock exposure on a leash.
QMFE: Options on the Nasdaq-100 set each February for a one year outcome period, absorbing a moderate slice of losses in exchange for capped gains. It cushions the tech heavy growth basket's famous swings, suiting investors who want Nasdaq exposure with a softer landing.
QMNV: Options on the Nasdaq-100 set each November for a one year outcome period, absorbing a moderate slice of losses in exchange for capped gains. It cushions the tech heavy growth basket's famous swings, suiting investors who want Nasdaq exposure with a softer landing.
RCLO: The middle layers of collateralized loan obligations: debt tranches rated in the BBB to B range, issued by vehicles bundling corporate loans. Those layers pay notably more than the safest CLO slices because losses reach them sooner, making this a yield hungry, credit heavy holding.
RILA: Growth stocks of any size picked aggressively, technology nearly half the fund with health care and consumer names behind, all chosen for their potential to expand fast. It is a go for growth holding that accepts big swings, suiting investors comfortable with an aggressive ride.
SDEM: Fifty emerging market companies in equal weights, chosen for ranking among the highest dividend payers in their markets, led by banks with consumer and energy names behind. Equal weighting lifts smaller payers to the same footing as giants, and the yields come with emerging market swings.
SOYB: Soybean futures contracts, rolled as they expire, giving direct exposure to the world soybean price without owning any physical beans. It is a single crop trading tool that swings with harvests, weather and export demand, and futures rolling costs can drag on long holdings.
SPIN: Large US stocks across every major industry, technology the biggest slice, paired with selling call options against the portfolio to collect premium income. It aims for stock market participation with fatter payouts, trading away part of strong rallies to keep the income coming.
SSXU: International stock funds weighted by a smart sector process that overweights and underweights countries and industries against a broad foreign benchmark. It is active allocation among funds rather than stock picking, so its edge depends on the country and sector calls landing right.
TENM: Options on large US stocks set each March for a twelve month outcome period, absorbing the first 10 percent of losses while capping gains. The buffer is the design target for each period, and the terms restart every March for the next round.
VDV: Value companies in developed markets outside the US: the cheaper, slower growing names across Europe, Japan and peers, led by banks, industrials and energy. It offers the value half of foreign investing, often with higher dividends, and trails when growth stocks abroad are in fashion.
WEEL: Sector funds and selected stocks paired with an option wheel: selling cash backed puts to collect income, and if assigned, selling covered calls on the shares until they are called away. The wheel turns market swings into a stream of option premiums, capping gains in strong runs.
XIDV: Dividend paying companies in developed markets outside the US, with the mix optimized to boost the dividend yield above a plain foreign index, led by banks and energy firms. It targets fatter payouts from abroad, accepting a tilt toward slower growing, cash heavy industries.
ZHOG: Bonds picked opportunistically across the market: government, corporate and mortgage debt, with managers free to shift maturities and quality as they hunt for value. It works as a flexible core income holding whose results depend on the managers' judgment calls about rates and credit.
